about: The words of the chain house_heir (encounters/chain_house_heir_793.json; the page is Design/content/chains/house_heir.md), written 6 Oct 2026 as a draft for the user to overwrite. Keys ch_house_heir.<step>.<what>; art.<card id> is one line for the artist on each card's picture. The heir is never named and never called son or nephew after the first card, because the same words must serve both; his own words are lines without a speaker. The one quotation is Hávamál 72 in H. A. Bellows's translation (The Poetic Edda, 1923), on the card of the oar. Nothing else is quoted: the sources behind each line are in the card's note.

entries.text: Three roofs

The widow who keeps the storehouse on the dam says the boy of your house knows every knot and one tongue, and that one tongue is a poor cargo. Three roofs would take him: the bishop's school, an English house, a Danish hearth.
Your boy sold my net-mender a dead eel as a sleeping one this morning. He is ready to be taught by someone who is not fond of him.
He is your son, born in the house on the dam, and he has been under every foot on it since he could walk.
He is your sister's son. She died on the mound in the fever year, a skipper brought him down the coast with a bundle and a comb, and the house has no other heir.
Saint Martin's at Traiectum has a school. He would come back able to read what the toll man cuts on his stick. He might also not come back: the bishop keeps the good ones.
Liudger went in at that door a Frisian boy and came out a bishop. I only say what is possible.
There is an Englishman above the Strand at Lundenwic who lodges our people and answers for them to the reeve. English is our own speech with a cold in its nose. He would have it by the second winter.

And there is the Dane at Ripa who speaks for Frisian ships. They foster each other's sons up there and think it binds two houses better than a marriage. Nobody else on this dam would have a Dane's door open to him.
He would come home with their gods on him somewhere. On a cord, or in his mouth when he swears. The priest will see it before you do.
My husband sent ours nowhere. He could gut a herring in the dark and could not ask for bread in any harbour but this one. Send the boy.
Take him to Traiectum, to Saint Martin's school
Take him to Lundenwic, to the English house
Take him to Ripa, to the Dane's hearth
Not this year
The master's bench

Inside the bishop's stone fort the master of Saint Martin's school looks the boy over as a man looks over a plank. He will take him. He asks what the house gives for his keep, and warns you what a good pupil costs a father.
A skipper's boy. Good. They can already count, and they have already been hit.
Franks, English, Frisians and Saxons have sat on that bench. They come in speaking four tongues and go out speaking one, badly.
At table he speaks Latin or he does not speak. For the first month he will be very quiet and very hungry. It passes.
The emperor's council wants the cloister schools kept for boys given to God. This is the bishop's school, not a cloister's. I take whom the bishop lets me take.
The boy has found a wax tablet on the bench and is pressing his thumbnail into it to see whether it holds a mark. It does. He looks at you as if he has found a flaw in a hull.
I tell you now, so that you do not shout at me later. If he is quick, the bishop will want him for the church. A boy who can read finds a boat small.
The church needs wax. For tablets, and for lights. And the master eats.
Give two cakes of wax and sixty pennies
Promise to carry the bishop's letters and bring him wax
Ask him to take the boy for God's sake
A house on the Strand

The Englishman who lodges Frisians above the Strand stands in his door with his own children behind him. He will keep the boy and answer for him to the reeve. He asks what the house gives, and says what a boy turns into here.
So this is the one. He looks like you about the ears. I am sorry for him.
Three nights under my roof and he is mine before the reeve. If he breaks a head, I pay for it first and come to you after. So I will be watching his hands.
First we find him a cloak that covers his knees. Your people sell us those little ones at the price of the big ones. I have not forgotten.
The boy is counting the ships drawn up on the strand below. He gets to forty, loses his place, and starts again without being told to.

I tell you now. At twelve winters the reeve counts him with my household when men are called out. And there are girls on this bank. If he comes home wanting to stay, that is your trouble and not mine.
He will eat like a hound. What comes with him?
Give a cask of Rhine wine for his table and forty pennies
Promise him first choice of your black stones
Say the boy will work for his bread
The Dane's knee

The Dane who answers for Frisian ships at Ripa sits by his fire with his own sons along the wall. Among his people a child is fostered by setting him on a man's knee. He waits to see whether you will ask, or pay, or simply do it.
You have brought me something that eats. Most Frisians bring me something that breaks.
With us, the man who raises another man's son is held the smaller of the two. So think how you do this. My sons are watching, and they will tell it for thirty years.
The boy is looking at the host's sons and they are looking at him. Nobody has blinked. The youngest of them is slowly holding out a piece of dried fish.
I tell you now. At the winter feast we eat horse, and he will sit at my table. He will swear by what my sons swear by, because boys do. What your priest makes of it is between you and your priest.
Well. The fire is warm and the knee is here.
Give a crate of glass for his table and thirty pennies' weight
Promise him the first of your wine each summer
Set the boy on his knee and say nothing of payment
Word of the boy
A skipper in from where the boy is has word of him for you, and gives it at the dam head with his eyes on his own mooring rope. The boy is well. The boy is also in trouble.
I saw your boy. He has grown. He has all his teeth. I was asked to tell you the rest as well.
He spoke Frisian at table. Twice. The second time he was beaten for it, and that night he was found at the river gate with his shoes in his hand, asking which boats went down to Dorestat.
The skipper hands you a wax tablet. There are five words cut in it in a careful, furious hand. He tells you what the master told him: four are right.
The host's nephew called him short-cloak in front of the other boys. Your boy broke his nose. It took two men to lift him off.
The host paid for the nose and says he was owed a laugh that cost that much. But he wants to know what you say, before the nephew's father asks him.
At the winter feast they put horse in front of him. He would not eat it. The men laughed. So he went out and sat in the snow by the boats until morning, and would not come in for anyone.
The host says a boy that stubborn is worth feeding. He also says the boy's feet were white, and that he wants a word from you, since he has only the one foster-son from the south.
And this, for nothing: the Danes' king has two hundred ships out, and they say he means them for the Frisian islands. Sell what you have lying north of here.
And this, for nothing: the old emperor is dead at Aachen, a week before Candlemas. His son has it all now. Charters will want showing again.
Whatever you send, send it by a man who will hand it to the boy and not to his keeper. A boy knows who a thing was given to.
Send him your own knife and one word: hold
Send word to his keepers: do not spare him
Send nothing. He must find his own feet
The school door

Three winters on. The boy comes out of the school door a hand taller, with ink on his thumb, and reads you the letters cut over the church door without being asked. The master stands behind him and does not want to let go.
"It says the house is Saint Martin's," he tells you. "It says it twice. They were afraid somebody would forget."
Your knife is on his belt, the sheath worn pale where his hand rests on it. He does not speak of it. He does not take his hand off it either.
He greets you in Latin first, correctly, and waits a breath too long before he says it again in Frisian.
He reads. He writes a hand I can bear to look at. He argues with the psalms about the price of things, which I did not teach him.
Your wax lit this church through two winters. I told the boy so, each time he thought himself forgotten.
A Bavarian wrote in his word-list that the Romans are fools and the Bavarians wise. That is what comes of learning a tongue from a list. Yours learned it from me.
The bishop has asked about him. I said he belongs to a boat. I said it once. I will not say it for you a second time.
On the way down to the boat he stops at the toll man's bench, looks at the tally lying there, and says quietly: "He has you down for two casks more than you landed."
Thank the master with sixty pennies for the church's lights
Take the boy and go
Leave him one more year
The tide on the Strand

Three winters on. You find the boy at the tide line beating an eel-wife down in her own tongue, and winning. He is a hand taller. The host comes down the bank behind him, in no hurry to give him back.
He sees you, finishes the bargain, takes the eels, and only then comes over. "She had them at three for a penny," he says. "They are four for a penny. Everybody here knows that but the Frisians."
Your knife is on his belt, the sheath worn pale where his hand rests on it. He does not speak of it. He does not take his hand off it either.
He greets you in English first, like a man of this bank, and waits a breath too long before he says it again in Frisian.
He can cheat a Kentishman in Kentish and a Mercian in Mercian. I have nothing left to teach him that I would want taught.
Your wine stood on my table at every feast since. I told the boy whose it was, each time he thought himself forgotten.
My own boy and yours are like two oars on one thwart. If you ever want him set up on this bank, I would not say no. I am only saying it.
The host's son walks down as far as the boat and stands with his hands in his belt. The two of them say nothing to each other for some time, in English.
Thank the host with forty-eight pennies and your hand
Take the boy and go
Leave him one more year
Down the beach

Three winters on. The boy comes down the beach at Ripa among the host's sons and you know him by his walk and by nothing else. He is a hand taller, he speaks as they do, and there is a small bone hammer on the cord beside his cross.
He sees you looking at the cord. "The cross is for the sea off our coast," he says. "The hammer is for the sea off theirs. I asked. Nobody could tell me where the one stops."
Your knife is on his belt, the sheath worn pale where his hand rests on it. He does not speak of it. He does not take his hand off it either.
He greets you in the Danes' tongue first, as a man of this beach, and waits a breath too long before he says it again in Frisian.
He rows. He can find the channel in fog by the smell of the mud. He still will not eat horse. I have stopped asking.
Your glass stood on my table at every feast since. I told the boy whose it was, each time he thought himself forgotten.
My sons go north in the spring for furs. They have a place on the thwart that is his size. I do not ask it. I say the place is there.
The host's sons carry his bundle down to the boat between them, though it weighs nothing. The eldest says one word to him. He says the same word back.
Thank the host with forty-eight pennies' weight and your hand
Take the boy and go
Leave him one more year
His first watch

Dusk, the wind backing, and broken water over a bar ahead. The boy has the steering oar for the first time, by your leave. The steersman says quietly that this is the place to take it back, if you mean to.
That bar is ugly on a backing wind. If she touches, she touches with your cargo in her. I say it once, and then it is your boat and your boy.
I had my first watch at twelve, running from York with half the city behind us. Nobody asked whether I was ready. I do not say that was better.
He has both hands on the oar and his feet planted wide, and he has not looked round at you once. That is either steadiness or fear. From behind they look the same.
His lips are moving. It may be a psalm. It may be the marks for this channel, said over in order. With him it is hard to know.
He is swearing at the bar under his breath, steadily, in English, as the men on the Strand swear at a tide that is late.
He has turned his face a little to feel the wind on his cheek, as the host's sons do, and he is reading the water by its colour and not by the marks.
Leave the oar in his hands
Stand behind him with your hand over his
Take the oar from him
The quarrel

A year on, in the house on the dam, with the boat laid up. He is of an age to answer for himself and he says so. He wants a share, and he wants his own way with it. The widow has come in for a light and is staying for the rest.
"I have been your hand since I could bail," he says. "I pull an oar for a hand's wage and I am told it is all mine one day. When is the day? I would like to know before I am old as well."

"You are cheated at every toll bench from here to the sea, because you cannot read what they write. Let me keep the house in ink. Or let me go back to Saint Martin, where at least they are cheated in Latin."
"Let me winter on the Strand and trade there on my own account, with the host's son. Wine up, wool down. You sell to the English like a man shouting across a river."
"My foster-brothers go north in spring. There is a thwart for me. One summer, and I come home with furs you have never had in this boat. You will not go past Ripa. I can."
"I brought her over the bar at dusk on a backing wind. You were there. You said nothing then, and you have said nothing since."
"You took the oar out of my hands at the bar, in front of the men. I have counted the days since. I can tell you the number."
"I touched her on the bar. Once. I have paid for that strake in my own head every night since. How long do I go on paying?"
"You sent word that I was not to be spared. They read it out to me. I thought you should know that they read it out."
The Franks let a boy answer for himself at fifteen winters. You answered for yourself at twelve, as I remember, and badly. Mind what you say next. He will carry it longer than you will.
The emperor has given each of his sons a portion while he is still alive to see what they do with it. If it is good enough for kings, it is good enough for a house with one boat.
Hear him to the end, and stake him: 120 pennies and a third of the next venture
He sails under you or not at all
Say nothing, and let the widow talk him down
The wrong side of the withy

Coming up to the dam at dusk you took the wrong side of the withy. The steersman laid his hand on the oar and said nothing until she was fast. Now he says it: your eyes are going, and the house must have another hand on the oar.
I will say the worst first. You did not see the withy. Last month you called the seal on the Maas bank a stone. It is your eyes, and they will not mend.
Tonight it was a stick and my hand was near. Next time it is a bank, and it is dark, and I am asleep. So. What can be done about it is in your house, eating your bread.
He is on the dam when you come ashore, with the tally of his own venture in his belt. It came home a third to the good. He has been waiting to see whether you would ask.

He is not on the dam. He went back to the roof that raised him the spring after the quarrel. When you send for him he comes by the first ship, and stands in the door, and does not sit until he is asked.
He is on the dam when you come ashore, and takes your line without a word, as he has every time since the quarrel. He does the work of two men and speaks like half of one.
My husband held his oar till the day he could not find the river with it. Then there was nobody to take it, and you know the rest. Do it while you can still see his face when you do.
The emperor put the crown on his son's head with his own hands, at Aachen, before all his great men. And he could still see.
The young emperor has shared the whole realm out among his sons already, in writing, and he is not forty. Nobody says he was too early. Yet.
The emperor's sons have risen against him this year, they say, because he would not say plainly what was whose. Say it plainly. It is cheaper.
The emperor's own sons have put him down, on a field in Alsace, and his men walked across to them in the night. That is what waiting buys.
Give him the steering oar, before witnesses
Divide the house: two keels, two hearths
Have the house set down in writing
Not yet: one more season
The steering oar

The dam head on a bright cold morning, with the men of the dams called to see it. You unship the steering oar and hold it out across the wale. What is given before witnesses stays given. It remains to say what the old man does next.
The oar is heavier out of its strap than it ever was in it. The loom is worn to the shape of your own two hands. You had not noticed that before today.
He takes it in both hands and does not say thank you. He turns it over and looks at the wear on the loom, and then he sets his hands exactly where yours were.
"I would have taken it from you kindly, two winters ago," he says, low, so the dam does not hear. "I take it all the same."
Let these men remember the day and the hour, and who stood where. Among the Franks they throw a stalk into the heir's lap. An oar is harder to lose.
There. Now you may come and sit in my storehouse door and tell the young ones the river was deeper in your day. I have kept a stool.
The Danes have a verse for it: "A son is better, though late he be born, and his father to death have fared; memory-stones seldom stand by the road save when kinsman honors his kin."
Hand it over, and keep the storehouse on the dam
Hand it over, and ship as his crew for one last summer
Hand it over, give a pound to Saint Martin and go under his roof
The oar is his. Every man on the dams who owed the house came to the ale and settled, so as to start clean with the new master. You keep the storehouse, and the stool in its door.
The oar is his. You pull the bow oar for him one whole summer and are told twice to keep stroke. In the autumn he hangs the old oar over the house door, where every heir after him will duck under it.
The oar is his. You give Saint Martin a pound of pennies and are given a bed, a bowl and a place at the back of the choir. The bishop's men know the house's boat now, and let her lie where she likes.
Two keels

The storehouse floor, swept, with everything the house owns laid out in three heaps and the widow holding the tally. One heap is his, and a keel of his own with it. It remains to say whether two keels are still one house.
Three heaps: cloth, casks, stones, and a small one of silver on top of each. Laid out like this the house looks smaller than it did, and also like more than you ever thought you had.
I have cut the tally three ways and I will swear to each of them. Two thirds stay on this dam. A third goes where he goes. Nobody is to move a cask until both of you have said yes aloud.
"Saint Martin has men who trade for him and pay no bank due here," he says. "I can be one of them, and still land your wax. The bishop gets a merchant who can read. You get a door in the stone fort."
"The host will let me a hearth above the Strand," he says. "Send me your wine and I will send you what it truly fetched. Nobody on that bank will tell a Frisian the price. They will tell me."
"My foster-father will have me land at his beach as one of his own," he says. "What comes down from the north comes to that beach first. I will be standing on it."
He does not look at you while the widow counts. He has brought silver of his own, from the roof that raised him, to buy what you would not give. He means to owe you nothing.
He looks from his heap to yours, and then moves one bolt of cloth from his to yours without a word. "That one was always the house's," he says.
Part as friends: he sails for Saint Martin and keeps your goods at Traiectum
Part as friends: he keeps a hearth above the Strand and your goods with it
Part as friends: he lands at his foster-father's and keeps your goods at Ripa
Let him buy the old boat and his third, and take the tally of it
Two keels, and one house still. He sails with the next fair wind. What he sends back the first season is more than his third was worth, and there is a door open to you now on another shore.
He counts out his foster roof's silver for the old boat and his third, takes his half of the tally stick, and sails. He will keep every bargain the stick names. He will not come to your ale.
The house in writing

A table by the church door with a calfskin leaf pegged flat on it, an ink horn, and the men of the dams standing well back from both. What the house owns, what it owes, who owes it, and whose it is next: all of it is to go down in ink.
Nobody on the dams has done this. Bishops do it, and counts, and the dead. The men have come to see whether a boat can be put on a calfskin, and whether anything will happen to you for trying.
A leaf with witnesses on it speaks in the count's court after every man here is dead. That is all the magic in it. Say the names slowly.
He cuts the pen himself and tries it on his thumbnail. "I will write it so a toll man can read it," he says. "Short words. Their Latin is worse than mine."
He stands at the priest's shoulder and makes him read each line back before the next is begun. He cannot read it. He can count the words, and he does.
Put me down for the storehouse rent, and put down that it is paid to Martinmas. If it is all going in ink, I want my part of it true.
When the names of those who owe the house are said aloud to be written, three men on the dam remember, quite suddenly, that they have the silver at home and can fetch it before the ink is dry.
Let him write it himself, with your share and his in it
Pay the priest sixty pennies to write it
Have it written twice, and lay one leaf in the church's chest: 120 pennies
The leaf is in his hand, with your share and his set side by side, and your mark under it drawn by you. He sews it into a cover of seal skin. It is the first leaf of the house's book.
The priest writes it and reads it back twice. Neither of you can read it. Both of you know now what it says, and so does the dam. It goes into the chest under the cloth.
Two leaves, cut from one skin along a wavy line so that each proves the other. One lies in the church's chest. The toll man hears of it and, for a year, takes your tally as you give it.
At Dorestat a skipper has given his steering oar to his heir at the dam head, before the men of the dams, while he still lives.
A house on the dam at Dorestat has been divided in three heaps on its own floor: the old man keeps two, and the heir has sailed with the third.
At Dorestat a skipper has had his whole house written on a calfskin, debts and all. Three men paid him the same day.

The dam head at Dorestat on a grey summer morning: a stout widow in a brown head-cloth pointing three ways with a tally stick, a thin priest beside her, and at their feet a boy of about ten sitting on a coil of rope, splicing it and listening.

A bare stone room inside the fort at Traiectum, morning light from one small window: a lean tonsured master on a bench, a row of wax tablets on the wall pegs, and a Frisian boy pressing his thumbnail into a tablet while his father stands in the doorway with two cakes of wax under his arm.

The gravel bank above the Strand at Lundenwic at low tide, afternoon, a wind off the river: a broad Englishman in a knee-length cloak in the door of a timber house with children behind him, and a boy in a short Frisian cloak counting the ships drawn up below.

A long Danish house at Ripa by firelight, evening: the host on a bench with one knee turned out, four sons along the wall, the youngest holding out a piece of dried fish to a small Frisian boy who stands very straight beside his father.

The dam head at Dorestat on a raw spring day: a weathered skipper looking down at his mooring rope while he holds out a small wax tablet, the merchant taking it, the widow watching from her storehouse door.

The door of Saint Martin's at Traiectum, a bright cold morning: a boy of about thirteen with ink on his thumb pointing up at letters cut in the stone lintel, his father looking at the boy and not the letters, the master in the shadow of the door behind them.

The tide line on the Strand at Lundenwic, early morning mist: a boy of about thirteen holding up four fingers to an eel-wife with a basket, ships beached behind, the host coming down the bank and the father standing unseen by a boat's stem.

The beach at Ripa in a pale spring noon: four Danish youths and one Frisian walking down the sand in a line, the Frisian known only by a cross and a small bone hammer on one cord, boats hauled up, the father waiting by his own.

The stern of a small open boat at dusk under a torn sky, wind backing, white water over a bar ahead: a boy with both hands on the steering oar and his feet wide, the steersman crouched at the sheet, the father standing a pace behind with one hand half raised.

Inside the house on the dam at Dorestat on a winter night, one tallow light: a youth of fifteen on his feet with his fists on the table, the merchant seated with his back to the wall, the widow in the door with an unlit lamp, snow blowing in behind her.

The channel below the dam at Dorestat at dusk, still water, a withy mark standing on the wrong side of the boat: the steersman's hand laid over the merchant's on the steering oar, the merchant peering ahead, the dam and its lights a blur.

The dam head at Dorestat on a bright cold morning, men of the dams in a half ring: the old merchant holding the unshipped steering oar out across the boat's side, the heir's two hands closing on its worn loom, the priest with a hand raised, the widow with a stool under her arm.

The swept floor of the storehouse on the dam, noon light from the open doors: cloth, casks and quern stones in three heaps with a little silver on each, the widow between them holding a split tally, father and heir on opposite sides, two boats seen on the river beyond.

A table by the church door at Dorestat on a still grey day: a calfskin leaf pegged flat, an ink horn, a hand with a quill, the old merchant making his mark, men of the dams standing well back, and three of them slipping away toward their houses.
